name: McKinsey $450B Projection
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Anatomy of a Number: Unpacking the $450 Billion Figure
lesson.summary: A widely cited McKinsey projection valuing quantum computing at roughly 450 billion dollars in the coming years illustrates, in one concrete case, exactly how the consulting-report methodology from the previous chapter produces a large, quotable number that outpaces demonstrated commercial reality.
lesson.body:
Among the consulting-firm projections discussed in the previous chapter, one figure attributed to McKinsey, reportedly valuing quantum computing's economic impact at somewhere in the neighborhood of 450 billion dollars within roughly the next decade or so, has circulated widely across industry conferences, startup pitch decks, and news coverage. I want to be explicit that I am not fully certain of the precise figure, year, or underlying report version, since McKinsey and similar firms have published multiple quantum technology market reports over the years with different headline numbers for different scopes, computing alone versus computing plus communication and sensing combined, and the exact figure circulating in a given context should be checked against the specific report being cited rather than assumed. What is worth examining is not whether this particular number is exactly right, but how a number like it gets built and why it deserves the scrutiny applied throughout this unit.

Figures of this kind are typically built the way the previous chapter described: by identifying industries where quantum computing might eventually offer an advantage, such as drug discovery, materials science, financial portfolio optimization, and logistics routing, estimating a plausible share of each industry's existing spending or value creation that quantum methods could eventually capture, and summing those estimates into one large headline number. This is a legitimate way to describe a scenario, but it rests on the assumption that fault-tolerant, error-corrected hardware arrives on the timeline the model assumes, an assumption the zero-ROI finding for 2025 and IBM's own roadmap revisions both suggest is far from settled.

It is worth stress-testing the number the way this unit has stress-tested every other claim in the catalog. What specific hardware milestone would need to occur, by what year, for that projected value to actually materialize. Does the underlying report name a required number of logical, error-corrected qubits, and a timeline consistent with the roadmap revisions IBM itself has already made. Reports of this kind rarely answer these questions with the precision they apply to the final dollar figure, which is itself informative: the headline number is usually far more confident than the technical assumptions that would need to hold for it to be realized.

This is not a case for dismissing the figure entirely. Quantum computing may well generate substantial economic value eventually, and estimating the scale of that eventual opportunity is legitimate work, in the same way early internet-era market projections, some of which turned out roughly right in the long run despite being wildly premature on their original timelines, were not worthless just because they arrived early. The issue is the gap between the confidence implied by a precise, large dollar figure and the genuine uncertainty in the technical assumptions feeding it.

Read against everything this unit has covered, from Feynman's 1981 proposal through Shor's algorithm, the early lab demonstrations, D-Wave's contested claims, Google's oversold supremacy result, IBM's repeatedly revised roadmap, and the absence of verified commercial ROI through 2025, a figure like this should be treated the way a careful reader treats any three-to-five-year claim: as one scenario among several, worth understanding for its assumptions, not as a settled forecast. That is the skeptical discipline this unit has been building toward, applied to the single most quoted number in the field.
